evmbench_critic_reasoning: Yes. The report explicitly flags the same bug: an unsafe uint256→uint96 downcast in Vault._burn used during withdraw/redeem, allowing a user with ≥ 2^96 shares (accumulated across multiple deposits) to burn only uint96(_shares) (truncating to 0 for 2^96) while withdrawing the full assets, then repeat to drain others’ funds. It references the same code path (withdraw → _withdraw → _burn at lines ~1138–1140), explains the same attack, and recommends the same fix (SafeCast.toUint96 / bounds check). Fixing that in the report would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly includes a finding titled “Missing access control in Vault.mintYieldFee allows any caller to steal accrued yield fee shares,” identifying that mintYieldFee lacks caller restrictions and allows minting to an arbitrary recipient instead of _yieldFeeRecipient. It references the same function and lines (394–402), same root cause (missing access control/recipient validation), and proposes the same remediation (restrict to _yieldFeeRecipient or remove the recipient parameter and always mint to _yieldFeeRecipient). Fixing as suggested in the report would fix the vulnerability described.

Yes. The report includes multiple findings that exactly match the described issue: a reentrancy via ERC721 onERC721Received that re-enters MinterContract.mint because NextGenCore.mint calls _safeMint (external interaction) before updating per-address mint counters (effects). Specifically, the findings titled “Reentrancy in NextGenMinterContract.mint Allows Bypassing Public Sale Per-Address Minting Limits” and especially “Reentrancy in NextGenCore.mint via _mintProcessing Allows Bypassing Per-Address Minting Limits” describe the same code path (MinterContract.mint -> NextGenCore.mint -> _safeMint -> onERC721Received -> reenter mint), the same root cause (CEI violation in NextGenCore.mint: tokensMintedAllowlistAddress/tokensMintedPerAddress updated after _safeMint), the same impact (bypass per-address limits and mint the entire supply), and the same fix (move counter updates before the external call and/or add a reentrancy guard). Fixing as suggested in the report would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report’s finding “Boundary Timestamp Overlap and Missing Bid Status Update in claimAuction Enables Duplicate Bid Settlement and Fund Draining” matches H-02 exactly. Both describe: (1) inclusive time checks (<= in cancelBid/cancelAllBids and >= in claimAuction) allowing both phases at block.timestamp == endTime; (2) claimAuction failing to set bid status = false for refunded bids; (3) an attacker calling claimAuction and then cancelBid/cancelAllBids in the same timestamp to obtain duplicate refunds (including refunding the winning bid), draining ETH and getting the NFT for free. The suggested fixes are the same: use strict inequality (>) in claimAuction and mark bids inactive (status = false) before/while refunding. Same mechanism, same code paths, and same remediation, so the vulnerability was detected.

Yes. The audit report explicitly identifies the same flaw in ProfitManager.claimGaugeRewards: when _userGaugeWeight == 0 the function returns early without checkpointing userGaugeProfitIndex to the current gaugeProfitIndex, enabling a user to vote after profits are accrued and then claim historical rewards (since userGaugeProfitIndex remains 0/1e18). It cites the same code path and lines, describes the same attack flow (enter/re-enter gauge, then claim to steal prior rewards), and proposes the same fix (always set userGaugeProfitIndex to the current gaugeProfitIndex even when weight is zero). Fixing the reported issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The report’s “Self-Transfer in ERC20RebaseDistributor.transfer Allows Rebasing Users to Mint Unbacked Tokens and Drain Unminted Rebase Rewards” describes the exact same bug as H-02: a self-transfer (to == msg.sender) while rebasing uses stale cached rebasingStateTo, causing toBalanceAfter to be computed from the old shares plus amount, which mints unbacked tokens from unmintedRebaseRewards and lets the caller steal all distributed (unminted) rewards. It cites the same code path (ERC20RebaseDistributor.transfer, lines ~559–632), the same mechanism (memory-cached rebasingState used after updating storage), the same impact (draining __unmintedRebaseRewards/stealing all rewards, inflating shares), and proposes the same class of fix (special-case or disallow self-transfers). Fixing the self-transfer caching issue as in the report would resolve H-02.

Yes. The audit report’s finding “Block Number and Timestamp Domain Mismatch in LendingLedger.update_market Causes Zero CANTO Reward Accrual” is the same issue as [H-01]. Both describe update_market passing a block-number-based epoch to GaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write, which expects a timestamp-aligned WEEK epoch, leading to zero/incorrect weights and thus broken reward accrual. They occur in the same code path (LendingLedger.update_market -> gauge_relative_weight_write), share the same root cause (block numbers used where timestamps are required), and would be fixed by the same remediation (align epochs to timestamps or map block epochs to timestamps).

Yes. The report contains a dedicated finding titled “Incorrect nextEpoch Calculation in LendingLedger.update_market Causes Cross-Epoch Reward Misattribution” that matches the described issue. Both specify that nextEpoch is incorrectly computed as i + BLOCK_EPOCH instead of epoch + BLOCK_EPOCH in update_market’s loop, causing cross-epoch reward misattribution/overpayment. They point to the same function/code path, the same underlying logic error, and propose the same fix (set nextEpoch = epoch + BLOCK_EPOCH). Fixing the report’s issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The report explicitly flags that Curves._transfer (used by transferCurvesToken, transferAllCurvesTokens, withdraw, deposit) updates balances without calling feeRedistributor.onBalanceChange for sender/recipient. It explains that FeeSplitter computes claimable using live balances and a stale (often zero) userFeeOffset, enabling repeated transfers to fresh accounts to claim historical fees and drain FeeSplitter. It proposes the same fix (call onBalanceChange/updateFeeCredit for both parties before balance mutation). This matches H-02’s root cause, code path, exploit, and remediation.

Yes. The report’s issue “Denial of Service in Curves._transferFees Allows Token Subject to Block Token Sales and Lock User Funds” is the same vulnerability as the HoneyPot attack. Both describe the same code path in Curves._transferFees where ETH is pushed to curvesTokenSubject and referralFeeDestination via low-level call and the transaction reverts on failure. Both note that referralFeeDestination can be arbitrarily set by the curve subject (setReferralFeeDestination) and that the call is executed even when referralFee == 0, enabling a malicious destination (or subject) to revert and thereby block sellCurvesToken, creating a honeypot where users can buy but cannot sell. Fixes proposed (use pull payments/handle failures instead of reverting, or safe send) would remediate the exact issue. Therefore, the audit detected the same vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report contains a specific finding titled “Missing access control in FeeSplitter.setCurves allows any caller to replace the Curves contract and drain all accumulated fees,” which matches the described vulnerability. Both identify that setCurves is publicly callable without access control, enabling an attacker to point to a malicious Curves contract, manipulate balances/supply, and inflate/withdraw fees. The location (FeeSplitter.setCurves), mechanism (missing access control), exploit path (replace curves, then claim), and remediation (restrict to onlyOwner/onlyManager) all align with the vulnerability description.

Yes. Both the audit content and the vulnerability description identify the same issue in Security.sol: the onlyOwner and onlyManager modifiers use equality checks as standalone statements without require/revert, thereby failing to enforce access control. They reference the same code locations (lines 8–11 and 13–16) and prescribe the same fix (wrap checks in require or revert). Fixing the modifiers as suggested would resolve both reports.

Yes. The audit includes a dedicated finding: “Missing Order Ownership Verification in MarginTradingHook.updateOrder Allows Arbitrary Order Modification…”, which states that updateOrder fails to verify order.initPosId == the caller’s initPosId, enabling arbitrary order edits. It references the same function and code path, identifies the same missing access control check, and proposes the identical fix (add _require(order.initPosId == initPosId,…)). Fixing that check would resolve both issues, so they are the same vulnerability.

Yes. The audit includes a dedicated finding: “Missing `_tokenOut` validation in `MarginTradingHook.updateOrder` allows setting arbitrary settlement tokens.” It identifies that `_createOrder` validates `tokenOut` but `updateOrder` does not, cites the same code region (L504–526), explains the same exploit (order creator front-runs to change `tokenOut` to an arbitrary/high-value token draining executors that pre-approve tokens), and proposes the same fix (require `_tokenOut` be either `baseAsset` or `quoteAsset`). This matches the described vulnerability exactly in mechanism, code path, attack, and remediation.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports the same issue under “In-place mutation in MarginTradingHook.updateOrder lets makers front-run and overcharge order fillers.” It explains that updateOrder mutates settlement-critical fields (including limitPrice_e36) on an active order under the same ID, allowing the order creator to front-run a pending fill and change the payout to overcharge/steal from the executor. It references the same code paths (updateOrder, _calculateFillOrderInfo, fillOrder), the same mechanism (front‑running by the order owner to change limitPrice_e36), and proposes the same class of fix (cancel-and-replace or version/hash checks). Fixing that reported issue would fix the vulnerability described.

Yes. The audit explicitly includes “Unvalidated Additional Seaport Consideration Items in Create.validateOrder Allow Renters to Poison RentalOrder.items and Permanently Lock Rented NFTs,” which matches the described issue: Seaport tipping lets a fulfiller append an ERC20 to consideration; Create.validateOrder/_processBaseOrderConsideration blindly include it in order items; later PaymentEscrow attempts to transfer the malicious token during stopRent, causing a revert and permanently locking the rental assets. The code path, mechanism, impact, and proposed fixes (binding to expected consideration items/count or order hash / disallow tips) align exactly with the reported vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly identifies and explains the same issue: the Safe’s setFallbackHandler (selector 0xf08a0323) is not blocked/validated by Guard, allowing a renter to set the fallback handler to the rented NFT contract and then invoke token functions via the Safe’s fallback path to bypass Guard and steal rented ERC721/1155 assets. Multiple sections (“Unguarded FallbackManager…”, “Missing setFallbackHandler Restriction…”, “Missing setFallbackHandler Selector Check…”) describe the exact attack path and propose fixes (block setFallbackHandler or ensure a fixed trusted handler), which would also remediate the vulnerability in the description. The mechanism, code path (Guard._checkTransaction and FallbackManager/setFallbackHandler), and fix are the same.

Yes. The report explicitly identifies the same root cause and exploit path: assets are transferred to the renter’s Safe before the rental is registered (Create.validateOrder/_rentFromZone updates Storage afterward), so Guard’s isRentedOut-based checks don’t apply yet. The report’s “Lifecycle-Dependent Protection Gap in Guard._revertSelectorOnActiveRental” explains that an attacker can use a callback such as onERC1155Received to re-enter and execute Safe transactions (e.g., transfer/approve) during this pre-registration window—exactly the ERC1155 hijack described. It also separately flags the missing restriction on setFallbackHandler, which enables the attacker to install a custom fallback handler to receive onERC1155Received on the Safe—matching the PoC mechanism. Fixes proposed (register before transfer or disallow such routes) would also fix the described issue. Therefore, the same vulnerability is detected in the same code path and mechanism.

Yes. The audit content explicitly flags the same composite issue: (1) Stop.stopRent executes external interactions (hook calls and Reclaimer.safeTransferFrom) before validating/removing the order in STORAGE, enabling a non-existent RentalOrder to be passed and the NFT to be transferred first; (2) the safeTransferFrom callback allows reentrancy where the attacker creates/fulfills a matching order during onERC721Received/onERC1155Received; and (3) Signer._deriveRentalOrderHash omits rentalWallet, letting the attacker supply the victim’s rentalWallet in stopRent while removeRentals later matches the attacker’s newly created order hash. The audit’s findings “Reentrancy and Unvalidated Order Execution in Stop.stopRent Allows Theft of Active Rented Assets” and “Missing rentalWallet field in Signer._deriveRentalOrderHash allows spoofing the rental wallet during stopRent,” together with the callback-driven reentrancy notes in Reclaimer, describe the same code path, mechanism, and fixes (move STORAGE check/cleanup before interactions, add reentrancy protections, and include rentalWallet in the order hash). This matches the reported exploit of stealing actively rented NFTs and freezing escrow on affected rentals.

Yes. The audit content explicitly describes the same flaw: Create._rentFromZone validates only zoneParams.totalExecutions in _executionInvariantChecks while it derives items from offer/consideration and then credits PaymentEscrow via increaseDeposit. By crafting self-transfers (to==from) or unmatched/missing executions, totalExecutions can be empty or incomplete, so no recipient checks run, yet storage and escrow are updated from offer/consideration. Later stopRent drains escrow. This matches H-06’s mechanism, code path (Create._rentFromZone, _executionInvariantChecks, _convertToItems, PaymentEscrow.increaseDeposit), attack (zero or missing executions due to Seaport ignoring self-transfers), and the proposed fix (verify recipients directly and ensure items match executions). Fixing what the report suggests would fix H-06 as well.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports that Storage.addRentals unconditionally sets orders[orderHash] = true, so multiple fulfillments producing the same orderHash (e.g., partial fills in the same block) will increment rentedAssets/escrow multiple times while Storage.removeRentals can only be called once, causing subsequent stops to revert with StorageModule_OrderDoesNotExist and leaving NFTs/ERC20 locked. It traces the same flow (Create._rentFromZone -> _deriveRentalOrderHash -> STORE.addRentals; later Stop.stopRent -> Storage.removeRentals) and proposes fixes (duplicate order check or ensuring unique order hash) that would also fix the described issue. Therefore, it is the same vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report explicitly flags that _beforeTokenTransfer pushes `to` into `holders` when balance is zero without checking `amount > 0` or `to != address(0)`, enabling zero-amount transfers and burns to bloat the `holders` array and create duplicate entries. It explains both consequences: duplicate entries leading to multiple reward payouts and DoS via unbounded growth. It proposes the same specific fix (only add when to != address(0) and amount > 0 and balanceOf(to) == 0). This is the same vulnerability, same code path, same mechanism, and same remediation as the described issue.

Yes. The audit content explicitly identifies the same TWAP manipulation flaw: _twapUpdate() is called after reserves/state are updated (via _setReserve/_sync/_resetTargetAndReserve), so the accumulator multiplies the elapsed time by the new post-trade price, allowing retroactive TWAP manipulation by the first transaction in a block. It references the same functions/code path (MagicLP._twapUpdate, _setReserve, _sync, etc.) and proposes the same fix (call _twapUpdate before modifying reserves/state or use the pre-mutation price). This matches the described vulnerability and attack scenario exactly.

Not detected. The reported issue is a rounding/logic bug in the initial-liquidity branch of MagicLP.buyShares: the comparison uses mulFloor in `quoteBalance < mulFloor(baseBalance, _I_)`, which can flip the branch and set shares = baseBalance, yielding targets B0/Q0 that violate the intended price ratio I (e.g., doubling the effective ratio). The proposed fix is to use mulCeil in the comparison so the min logic is correct near the boundary.

While the audit content covers many buyShares problems (unbalanced initial deposits leading to reserve–target desync, prefunded bootstrap theft, decimal-dependent minimum liquidity, precision loss and under-minting during normal deposits, etc.), none specifically identifies this initial-condition rounding error or recommends changing that comparison to mulCeil. The highlighted buyShares findings focus on different root causes and fixes (e.g., refunding excess tokens, proportional reserve updates, share-minting attribution), which would not correct the I-invariant break caused by the mulFloor-based comparison. Therefore, fixing the audit’s issues would not necessarily fix the vulnerability described in H-02.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports the same issue: BlastOnboardingBoot.bootstrap passes the full, potentially imbalanced locked MIM/USDB amounts to Router.createPool, which transfers both tokens in full and calls MagicLP.buyShares. buyShares sets targets from the minimum side while recording full balances as reserves, creating a reserve–target mismatch that can be immediately arbitraged to extract the excess side. The audit’s first item (“Imbalanced MIM and USDB Locked Totals… Allow Immediate Drainage of Excess Pool Reserves”) and the second item (“Insufficient Slippage and Liquidity Balance Validation… Skewed Pool Initialization”) both trace the exact code path (BlastOnboarding.deposit/lock → bootstrap → router.createPool → MagicLP.buyShares → PMMPricing) and show how an attacker can drain the imbalance. The proposed fix (use previewCreatePool to adjust amounts or rebalance before enabling trading) would also fix the described vulnerability. Thus, the report detected the same vulnerability in the same functions and mechanism.

Yes. The report’s section “Spot Reserve Manipulation in MagicLpAggregator.latestAnswer Allows Flash-Loan Inflation of LP Token Price” describes the same issue as the vulnerability: MagicLpAggregator.latestAnswer derives price from spot reserves (baseReserve + quoteReserve)/totalSupply, which can be skewed via flash loan/large swaps, inflating the LP price. It points to the same function and code path, the same manipulation mechanism, and a fix (change how price is derived to non-manipulable targets) would also resolve the issue described. Thus, the audit report detected the same vulnerability.

Yes. The report explicitly describes the same issue: excess msg.value is not refunded in ASDRouter._sendASD. It covers both branches—local transfer (msg.value ignored) and cross-chain send (only _feeForSend forwarded; remainder stuck)—and notes no withdrawal path, matching the described stuck native gas token vulnerability. The suggested fix (refund surplus or forward full msg.value) would fix the vulnerability as reported. Same function/code path, mechanism, and remediation.

Yes. The audit content explicitly identifies the same issue: ASDRouter.lzCompose is callable by anyone (no msg.sender check against the LayerZero endpoint) in a separate transaction after tokens are already credited, enabling arbitrary callers to forge parameters and steal the bridged funds. It references the exact function/path (ASDRouter.lzCompose), the same two-step LayerZero composed flow, and proposes the same fix (restrict lzCompose to the trusted LZ endpoint). Fixing the audit-reported issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly flags that removeOwnerAtIndex is whitelisted for cross-chain replay via executeWithoutChainIdValidation, and because owners are identified solely by index, index divergence across chains can cause replayed removals to delete a different owner (including potentially the last/only owner, bricking the wallet). It references the same code path (CoinbaseSmartWallet.canSkipChainIdValidation, validateUserOp, and MultiOwnable.removeOwnerAtIndex), describes the same mechanism (index-only binding with cross-chain replay), the same impact (unintended/last-owner removal and bricking), and proposes the same fix (bind the owner bytes in removeOwnerAtIndex). Fixing as the report suggests would also fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report’s item “Missing userTotalStaked update in IdentityStaking.release” is the same vulnerability: in release(), stake amounts are increased but userTotalStaked is not, breaking the userTotalStaked invariant and causing underflow/locked funds on withdrawals and potential DoS on subsequent slashes. It references the same function/lines, mechanism, impact, and proposes the same fix (increment userTotalStaked by amountToRelease). Fixing it as suggested would resolve the described H-01 issue.

Yes. The audit explicitly describes the same issue: in vote_for_gauge_weights, after allowing _user_weight == 0 for removed gauges, it then computes gauge_type = gauge_types_[_gauge_addr] - 1 and requires gauge_type >= 0 (lines ~401–402), which always reverts for removed gauges (gauge_types_ == 0). This prevents users from withdrawing their vote, permanently locking their vote_user_power. The audit’s “Contradictory Gauge Type Validation in vote_for_gauge_weights Prevents Withdrawing Votes from Removed Gauges” section matches the reported vulnerability in mechanism, function, and fix (remove the redundant require), so fixing the audit’s finding would fix the described issue.

Yes. The report’s second finding (“Repeated Gas Issuance Deduction in TaikoL2._calc1559BaseFee Due to Threshold-Delayed lastSyncedBlock Updates”) describes the same root cause and code path as H-01: _calc1559BaseFee computes issuance as (_l1BlockId − lastSyncedBlock) * gasTargetPerL1Block while anchor only updates lastSyncedBlock when _l1BlockId > lastSyncedBlock + BLOCK_SYNC_THRESHOLD (5). This causes over-issuance (repeated deduction), deflating basefee and potentially causing a mismatch with block.basefee that could halt the chain. The proposed remediation (track last anchored L1 block or update lastSyncedBlock on every anchor and use that for issuance) would fix H-01 as well. Thus, the same vulnerability is detected.

Yes. The audit content flags the same core flaw: bonds for non-selected/overwritten transitions are effectively lost (economically “burned”/frozen) with no path to refund even when the ultimate, finalized outcome shows those earlier actions were correct. In particular, “Unsettled fork bonds in TaikoL1.verifyBlocks let malicious provers burn larger contest bonds” explains that only the selected transition is settled in verifyBlocks while other transitions’ validity/contest bonds remain unreconciled, matching the report’s examples where a prover’s or contester’s bond is lost after later top-tier resolution. It cites the same code paths (LibProving._overrideWithHigherProof resetting state; LibVerifying.verifyBlocks paying only the final ts.prover) and complements this with “Premature liveness-bond settlement…” showing the top-tier path can only refund liveness, not validity/contest bonds—precisely the limitation called out in H-02. A fix that adds refund/claim handling for non-selected/overridden transitions (as the audit suggests) would also resolve the described wrongful slashing when the final verified transition vindicates earlier actions.

Yes. The report’s first finding describes the same logic flaw in ERC20Airdrop2: the ongoingWithdrawals modifier reverts when block.timestamp > claimEnd + withdrawalWindow, while full vesting only completes at claimEnd + withdrawalWindow. This makes it practically impossible to withdraw 100% unless the tx lands exactly at that timestamp and blocks all withdrawals afterward. It references the same modifier and withdraw() code path and suggests removing the upper bound or adding a grace period—fixes that would resolve the described H-03 issue.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports that params.coinbase in LibProposing.proposeBlock is caller-controlled and then used by AssignmentHook.onBlockProposed to pull ERC20 fees via safeTransferFrom(_meta.coinbase, _blk.assignedProver, proverFee) without verifying that coinbase is the proposer or consented. This allows a proposer to set coinbase to any victim who has approved the hook and force them to pay the prover’s fee—exactly the issue described. The proposed fixes (bind coinbase to msg.sender or require proposer authorization/signature) also match the remediation in the description. Therefore, the same vulnerability and code path are identified.

Yes. The audit explicitly identifies the same replay issue in TimelockTokenPool.withdraw(address,bytes): the signed message only includes a static string and _to, lacking a nonce/domain separation, allowing indefinite re-use of the same signature to withdraw future unlocks. It references the exact function and code path, explains repeated withdrawals with the same sig, and proposes adding a nonce/deadline/EIP-712—fixes that would also resolve the reported vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report’s “Incorrect Decimal Scaling in ChainlinkOracleConnector.getValueFromChainlinkFeed” section describes the same flaw as H-01: incorrect handling of decimals when using Chainlink feeds, especially when routing through ETH/USD. It pinpoints that getValue/getValueFromChainlinkFeed use the feed’s decimals (and even substitute ETH/USD with the aggregator address for decimals) causing outputs to be in the wrong units (e.g., ETH decimals instead of USD), and provides a scenario where ETH/USD (8 decimals) causes a 10-decimal error—exactly matching H-01’s ETH/USD multi-hop case. The code paths and fix (proper normalization using asset/baseToken decimals and feed.decimals, treating ETH as 18 and USD as 8) would also fix H-01. The other two findings are different issues, but the second clearly detects H-01.

Yes. The report’s first finding describes the exact same bug: in NoyaValueOracle._getValue’s loop, it incorrectly passes asset instead of the evolving quotingToken for multi-hop routes, causing reverts or incorrect valuations. It points to the same code lines and proposes the same fix (use quotingToken inside the loop). Thus, fixing the report’s issue fixes the described vulnerability. The second finding in the report is a different issue and does not affect this match.

Yes. The audit content explicitly identifies head-of-line blocking in AccountingManager.executeWithdraw caused by baseToken.safeTransfer to a user-controlled receiver that may revert, including when the receiver is blacklisted on tokens like USDC/USDT. It references the same function and code path (executeWithdraw -> safeTransfer to data.receiver), the same mechanism (transfer revert due to blacklist causing FIFO queue to halt), and proposes fixes (validate receiver/handle transfer failures) that would also remediate the described blacklist-based DoS.

Yes. The audit explicitly flags PendleConnector.depositIntoMarket transferring full SY/PT to the market, then calling market.skim(), explaining that skim sends surplus to the Pendle treasury, causing loss of unused tokens. It ties the loss to reserve ratio changes/MEV and recommends routing via the Pendle router or pre-calculating used amounts (and effectively not relying on skim). This is the same mechanism, code path, and fix as the described vulnerability.

Yes. The report explicitly identifies that AerodromeConnector._getPositionTVL only uses IERC20(pool).balanceOf(address(this)) and ignores LP tokens staked in the gauge (IGauge(gauge).balanceOf(address(this))). It details how stake transfers LP to the gauge, causing TVL underreporting, and recommends including the gauge-staked balance in _getPositionTVL. This is the same function, code path, root cause, and fix as the described [H-06] issue.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports the same issue: in PendleConnector.burnLP the call market.burn(address(this), address(market), amount) incorrectly sets the PT receiver to the market instead of address(this), causing loss of PT. It points to the exact function and call site, explains the impact, and proposes the same fix (use address(this) as receiverPt). Fixing as suggested in the report would also fix the vulnerability described in H-07.

Yes. The report explicitly identifies the same cross‑vault privilege escalation via BalancerFlashLoan + BaseConnector.sendTokensToTrustedAddress(). It points to the same code path (BaseConnector.sol lines allowing msg.sender == registry.flashLoan()) and the same mechanism: a keeper of one vault invokes BalancerFlashLoan with destinationConnector set to another vault’s connector, which then calls sendTokensToTrustedAddress on that other connector and drains tokens. The report’s PoC and impact match the warden’s description, and the proposed remediations (scoping flash-loan targets to the validated vault and/or tightening sendTokensToTrustedAddress authorization) would fix the described issue.

Yes. The report’s Finding 6 explicitly states that after an external closure (including Recovery Mode liquidation), surplus collateral is credited to TroveManager.surplusBalances and PrismaConnector exposes no function to claim it, leaving the surplus unclaimed. It recommends adding a managed function in PrismaConnector to call Prisma’s surplus claim, which is the same fix as adding a wrapper to TroveManager.claimCollateral. This matches the described H-09 root cause (missing claim function) and the same code path/state. The report also discusses valuation side effects, but it clearly identifies and proposes a fix for the inability to claim surplus collateral.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports the same issue: when resetMiddle rolls back the withdrawal queue, currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount is not adjusted, so subsequent calculateWithdrawShares re-adds amounts, inflating totalCBAmount and potentially bricking/underpaying withdrawals. This is described in the sections “Recalculation of Withdrawals … After resetMiddle Double-Counts currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount” and “Incomplete Rollback of currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount in AccountingManager.resetMiddle Causes Double-Counting of Withdrawal Amounts,” referencing the same functions/lines. The proposed remediations (resetting/adjusting totalCBAmount on reset or subtracting prior amounts) would also fix the vulnerability in the description, which suggests setting totalCBAmount to 0. Therefore, the reported vulnerability matches the described one in mechanism, code path, and fix.

Yes. The report explicitly flags the same SNXConnector TVL miscalculation in the same functions. It includes two findings that match the description: (1) “Unaccounted Synthetix V3 Debt in SNXConnector.mintOrBurnSUSD and SNXConnector._getPositionTVL Inflates Vault TVL,” which describes failing to subtract the sUSD debt created by mintUsd (same root cause and code path), and (2) “Double Counting of Delegated Collateral in SNXConnector._getPositionTVL,” which points out summing totalDeposited + totalAssigned even though totalDeposited already includes totalAssigned. Both issues are in SNXConnector._getPositionTVL and mintOrBurnSUSD, and the proposed remediations (subtract debt; use only totalDeposited) align with fixing the reported vulnerability. Additional nuances about internal Synthetix accounting are extra but do not change that the same vulnerability was detected.

Yes. The audit report’s item “Ownership and calculator connector identity conflation in PositionRegistry.updateHoldingPosition…” describes the exact same bug: during removal when swapping the last element into positionIndex, the code updates isPositionUsed using calculatorConnector instead of ownerConnector to recompute the holdingPositionId. It pinpoints the same function/path (Registry.updateHoldingPosition removal branch), same mechanism (wrong key for mapping after swap), same impact (corrupted index -> broken TVL), and same fix (use ownerConnector in the hash). Fixing that in the report would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The report’s “Incorrect BPT Valuation Formula in BalancerConnector._getPositionTVL” flags the same issue: the valuation in _getPositionTVL is wrong, specifically because it relies on a single token’s balance and divides by the token’s weight, which mismatches Balancer’s valuation approach and leads to mispricing. It references the exact same function/lines and proposes removing the weight-based division and summing underlying token values (and also correcting supply via getActualSupply). Although the report also covers additional problems (single-token spot manipulation and totalSupply vs getActualSupply), fixing as recommended would also fix the misuse-of-weight error described in the vulnerability. Same code path, mechanism, and effective fix.

Yes. The audit content includes “Incorrect BPT Supply Query in BalancerConnector._getPositionTVL” which flags the exact issue: using IERC20(pool.pool).totalSupply() instead of Balancer’s getActualSupply() for pre-minted BPT pools, causing severe TVL miscalculation. It cites the same function (BalancerConnector._getPositionTVL), same code path, same root cause, same impact (invalid TVL/position valuation), and proposes the same fix (use getActualSupply). Fixing it as suggested would resolve the vulnerability described in H-14.

Yes. The audit content explicitly flags “Incorrect share-to-asset valuation in SiloConnector._getPositionTVL,” pointing to the same function and code path. It explains that collateralToken/collateralOnlyToken/debtToken are share tokens and that _getPositionTVL wrongly uses their raw balances (and a 1e18 unit price) instead of converting shares to underlying amounts before pricing, which miscalculates TVL and thus share pricing. The proposed fix (convert each share balance to underlying using Silo math/interest, then sum and value) would also fix the H-15 issue. Therefore, the report detected the same vulnerability described.

Not detected. The audit content lists multiple issues (registry indexing bugs, authorization/trust gaps, valuation errors, inverted health-factor semantics, solvency checks in withdraw/repay, etc.), but none state that SiloConnector.borrow lacks a post-borrow solvency check. The reported items focus on withdraw and repay checks (including suggesting removing the repay check), not on adding a solvency check to borrow. Fixes proposed in the audit would not add the missing borrow-time check, so they would not resolve the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly includes “Incorrect removePosition Flag in DolomiteConnector.openBorrowPosition Causes Unregistered Borrow Positions,” describing the same root cause (passing removePosition = true to Registry.updateHoldingPosition), in the same function/code path (DolomiteConnector.openBorrowPosition), with the same effect (position never registered; omitted from TVL), and the same remediation (pass false instead). Fixing the issue as described in the report would fix the vulnerability in the description.

Yes. The audit report clearly identifies the same MorphoBlue TVL-calculation errors called out in the description: (1) it flags and demonstrates that _getPositionTVL adds borrowAmount instead of subtracting it (Finding 9), matching point 2 in the description and proposing the same fix; and (2) it points out that withdraw updates the registry only for the collateral token and not the loan token (Finding 6), matching point 3 with the same specific fix. The report also contains multiple other Morpho TVL issues. While it does not explicitly cover the decimals-handling problem in convertCToL (point 1), the core vulnerability class and exact code paths for points 2 and 3 are the same, and the proposed fixes would resolve those specific issues as described.

Yes. The audit content includes “Premature Position Closure in PendleConnector.decreasePosition Due to Omitted Penpie Staked LP Balance Check,” which describes the same flaw: decreasePosition uses isMarketEmpty that doesn’t check Pendle LP staked in Penpie (pendleMarketDepositHelper.balance), causing premature removal of the holding position and TVL omission. It cites the same code paths (decreasePosition and isMarketEmpty) and proposes the same fix (include the Penpie staked balance in the emptiness check). Fixing as suggested in the report would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content includes a specific issue: “Incorrect Denomination Aggregation in PendleConnector._getPositionTVL Causes Double-Scaling of LP and PT Positions by SY.exchangeRate()”. It explains that getLpToAssetRate and getPtToAssetRate already return values in underlying-asset units, yet the code adds them to SYAmount (SY units) and then multiplies by SY.exchangeRate, causing incorrect TVL. This is the same root cause and code path as the reported [H-22] finding (misinterpreting getLpToAssetRate/getPtToAssetRate as SY-priced), and the proposed fix (add LP/PT values directly to underlyingBalance rather than SYAmount) would resolve both. Therefore, the report detected the same vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report has a dedicated finding titled “Missing Holding Position Synchronization in DolomiteConnector.transferBetweenAccounts Causes Inaccurate Vault TVL,” which describes that transferBetweenAccounts moves balances between account 0 and a sub-account without updating PositionRegistry holding positions. This matches the described issue exactly: same function (DolomiteConnector.transferBetweenAccounts), same mechanism (not updating holding positions for account 0 and accountId), same impact (inaccurate TVL), and the same remediation (call registry.updateHoldingPosition for both accounts based on whether each has markets/balances). Fixing the report’s issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report explicitly captures the same issue via two findings that together mirror the H‑01 scenario and root cause: (1) “Insufficient Stake Enforcement Across baseStake Decreases…” explains that after a baseStake decrease, a child can be created with a smaller requiredStake, which unlocks the higher stake on the unconfirmed parent once firstChildBlock > 0, leading to collateral shortfalls/drainage. This occurs in the same code path: RollupUserLogic.stakeOnNewAssertion (checks only parent’s requiredStake at line ~182, transfers to loserStakeEscrow at ~210–216) and RollupCore.createNewAssertion (snapshots live baseStake into the child). (2) “Premature Inactive‑Staker Classification in requireInactiveStaker” describes that a staker is considered inactive as soon as their latestStakedAssertion has a child (firstChildBlock > 0) even if unconfirmed (RollupCore.requireInactiveStaker ~565–574), enabling the parent’s staker to withdraw the higher stake prematurely. This is exactly the H‑01 step where Bob creates G (lower stake) to set firstChildBlock and let Alice withdraw her higher stake, leaving the contract insolvent because loserStakeEscrow already received the higher amount. The recommended fixes (enforce inactivity only on confirmation and/or ensure child requiredStake can’t drop below ancestors) align with H‑01’s suggested remediations. Fixing these audit‑reported issues would also fix H‑01.

Yes. The report’s “Reentrancy and Shared ETH Balance Consumption in _claim” finds the same core flaw: in PrelaunchPoints._claim the contract mints/stakes lpETH using claimedAmount = address(this).balance rather than the exact ETH obtained from the user’s swap. This is the same code path and root cause exploited in H-01’s Scenario 1 (donate ETH + claim to capture donated ETH), and the proposed fix is identical (use the exact ETH delta returned from _fillQuote/buyAmount rather than address(this).balance). Although the report frames exploitation via reentrancy/partial claims, it targets the same mechanism and fix; correcting it would also prevent the donation + claim bypass. The report does not cover Scenario 2 (convertAllETH sandwich/ratio manipulation), but it still detects the key vulnerability described in H-01 Scenario 1.

Yes. The audit’s second finding (“Unrestricted LockManager.lockOnBehalf allows any caller to reset a player's lock state … and lock funds indefinitely”) is the same issue. Both describe lack of access control on lockOnBehalf, ability to call with zero amount, and the resulting reset of lastLockTime/unlockTime that indefinitely pushes a victim’s unlock time, preventing withdrawals. They reference the same code path (lockOnBehalf -> _lock setting unlockTime) and propose the same fix (restrict to MigrationManager/authorization). Fixing the audited issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content’s item “Inconsistent unlockTime Calculation in LockManager.setLockDuration Allows Players to Reduce Existing Lockup Times and Unlock Early” describes the exact same issue as [H-02]: in setLockDuration, the validation compares block.timestamp + _duration against current unlockTime while the assignment sets unlockTime = lastLockTime + _duration. This mismatch lets users reduce unlockTime (even to <= now) and unlock early. It cites the same function/lines, demonstrates the same attack path, and proposes the same specific fix (use the same base for validation and assignment, e.g., validate lastLockTime + _duration or reset from block.timestamp). Fixing the report’s issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports the same root cause and code path: after removeNominee, pointsSum[nextTime].slope is not reduced (only bias is), and revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower cancels scheduled changes without removing the active slope. Sections “Missing Slope Deduction in VoteWeighting.removeNominee Corrupts pointsSum and Inflates Relative Weights” and “Desynchronized Slope Cancellation and Missing Checkpoint in revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower” match H-01’s mechanism and locations (removeNominee and _getSum, plus revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower). Both describe how _getSum continues using an inflated slope, corrupting totals, and propose the same fix: subtract the nominee’s slope from pointsSum (and/or adjust in revoke). Fixing as suggested in the report would fix H-01.

Yes. The audit includes “Unauthenticated Cross-Chain Origin in GnosisTargetDispenserL2.onTokenBridged Bypassing DefaultTargetDispenserL2._receiveMessage Checks,” which matches the described issue exactly: onTokenBridged() does not authenticate the L1 sender/token and passes hardcoded relayer/processor to _receiveMessage, allowing anyone via OmniBridge relayTokensAndCall to inject arbitrary data that _processData then executes—distributing OLAS or creating redeemable queue entries. The code path (GnosisTargetDispenserL2.onTokenBridged -> _receiveMessage -> _processData) and impact align, and the proposed fix (remove onTokenBridged/use authenticated AMB path) is the same. Fixing the reported issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. Both describe the same logic error in the exact-output path of sellCreditMarket (params.exactAmountIn == false), specifically in AccountingLibrary.getCreditAmountIn. The fee is incorrectly computed using cashAmountOut * swapFeePercent / PERCENT instead of charging on the gross amount (dividing by PERCENT - swapFeePercent) and, in the fractional case, omitting fragmentationFee from the fee basis. Both reference the same code lines (L249, L256) and propose the same fix (use denominator PERCENT - swapFeePercent and include fragmentationFee in the numerator when fractionalized). Fixing as proposed in either would fix the other.

Not detected. The described issue is a transaction-ordering/race between repay and liquidateWithReplacement caused by repay identifying a position only by debtPositionId and not binding to the borrower, allowing a user’s repay to clear a different borrower’s debt if replacement executes first. The proposed fix is to include and check the borrower address in Repay. None of the audit findings cover this mechanism: the Repay-related items address scaled-share rounding/underfunded transfers, and the LiquidateWithReplacement items address issuance rounding, due-date restoration, rounding additivity, and offer reuse. No item mentions the borrower-identity check, the TOCTOU/race with replacement, or proposes the same fix, so fixing the reported issues would not fix H-02.

Yes. The audit report includes a dedicated finding: “Incorrect collateralRemainderCap calculation in Liquidate.executeLiquidate overcharges borrowers on overdue liquidations.” It identifies the same function and code path (Liquidate.executeLiquidate), the same flawed formula (using debtInCollateralToken * crLiquidation / PERCENT as the remainder cap instead of only the excess over 100%), the same impact (overcharging/penalizing higher-CR borrowers during overdue liquidations), and proposes the same class of fix (cap by the excess, e.g., using crLiquidation - PERCENT or capping total collateral at crLiquidation then subtracting the liquidator amount). Fixing the issue as described in the report would fix the vulnerability described in H-03.

Yes. The audit explicitly reports that in Liquidate.executeLiquidate the liquidatorReward is computed using debtPosition.futureValue (6‑decimals debt token) instead of debtInCollateralToken (18‑decimals collateral token), causing severe underpayment. It cites the exact code path (lines ~95–103), explains the decimals/denomination mismatch, and recommends fixing by basing the reward on debtInCollateralToken. This is the same mechanism, location, impact, and fix as the H‑04 description.

Yes. The report explicitly flags the same flaw in THORChain_Router._routerDeposit: it approves an arbitrary target router for a nominal amount and neither verifies that depositWithExpiry actually pulls the tokens nor revokes any unspent allowance, leaving a lingering approval against the router’s pooled custody. This enables a malicious router to later call transferFrom and drain funds (including those later deposited by others), which is exactly the mechanism used in the H-01 description. The report’s sections “Unsafe Token Approval Lifecycle in _routerDeposit…” and “Unverified Cross-Router Token Settlement and Allowance Handling in _routerDeposit” describe the identical code path (transferAllowance → _routerDeposit → safeApprove + external depositWithExpiry), the same root cause (residual approval to untrusted router and no verification of actual transfer), and propose the matching fix (zero-reset approvals, verify balance deltas/consumption, revoke remaining allowance). Although H-01 highlights a rebasing token (AMPL) to illustrate impact, the attack relies on the same residual-approval flaw that the report identifies; fixing the report’s issue would also fix H-01.

Yes. The audit report explicitly identifies that THORChain_Router.transferOut uses to.send(...) and, even on failure (with ETH bounced back to the vault), still unconditionally emits TransferOut(msg.sender, to, asset, safeAmount, memo). This is the same flaw described: incorrect event emission on failed native ETH sends causes THORChain to treat unsuccessful outbounds as successful. It cites the same function and lines, the same mechanism (2300-gas .send bounce then misleading event), and proposes equivalent fixes (use .call/revert or adjust event to reflect actual recipient). Fixing the report’s issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit’s first issue precisely matches H-01. Both identify that ILOPool.claim uses a shared Uniswap V3 position, calls pool.collect with type(uint128).max, and then transfers amountCollected - amount to the fee taker, thereby sweeping other users’ accrued fees. This causes subsequent claims to lack available fees and revert (often via SafeTransfer "ST" or underflow in 0.7.6). The code path and root cause are the same (ILOPool.claim with burn/collect on the shared position), the attack scenario is identical (first claimant drains others; later claimers fail), and the proposed remediation is the same (collect only the amounts attributable to the claiming tokenId rather than max). Fixing the audit-reported issue would fix H-01.

Yes. The audit report’s first finding (“Spot Price Manipulation in ILOManager.launch Enables Denial of Service of Project Launch”) is the same issue as [H-03]. Both identify the strict equality check in ILOManager.launch against Uniswap V3’s slot0.sqrtPriceX96 and explain that the pool is publicly mutable pre-launch, allowing an attacker to move the price (via swaps) and further entrench it (e.g., by adding concentrated/single‑sided liquidity), making restoration to the exact cached price infeasible and causing the launch to revert. The code path (ILOManager.launch), mechanism (price manipulation leading to failed equality check), and remediation (restore price or initialize at launch/avoid early init) align. Fixing the audit’s issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report explicitly includes a finding titled “Missing onlyOwner Access Control in WellUpgradeable._authorizeUpgrade Allows Unauthorized Contract Upgrades,” which states that _authorizeUpgrade lacks onlyOwner, allowing any address to call upgradeTo/upgradeToAndCall. It references the same function and mechanism, demonstrates a PoC of non-owners upgrading, and prescribes the same fix (adding onlyOwner). Fixing the reported issue would fix the described vulnerability, so they are the same.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports the same bug in Stable2.decodeWellData: the second zero-check mistakenly tests decimal0 again instead of decimal1, so decimal1 never defaults to 18 when encoded as 0, causing mis-scaling. It points to the same code path, explains the same impact (reserve/price distortions), and proposes the same fix (change the second condition to if (decimal1 == 0) { decimal1 = 18; }). Fixing the issue as in the report would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports the same bug: in stake(), protocolDeposit for Lido/Etherfi returns shares while getAccountTotalUnstakedYield/getAccountYieldBalance reads rebased token balances (stETH/eETH). This unit mismatch is used in _convertToYieldSharesWithTotalYield/convertToYieldShares, causing misallocation across multiple NFTs in the same YieldAccount (earlier stakes over-credited, later under-credited), enabling excess withdrawal for some NFTs and pushing others toward liquidation. The audit sections “Share-to-Asset Unit Mismatch in YieldStakingBase._stake and protocolDeposit…” and “Share-Versus-Token Denomination Mismatch in YieldEthStakingEtherfi.protocolDeposit…” match the exact code path and mechanism cited in the description and propose the same fix (return/measure actual token balance delta instead of shares). Fixing as recommended in the report would also fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content includes “Unvalidated onBehalf Parameter in IsolateLending.isolateRepay…” which matches exactly: missing validation that onBehalf equals the NFT owner during isolateRepay, leading to decrementing the wrong user’s userScaledIsolateBorrow and underflow on later repay/liquidate/redeem. It points to the same code path (ValidateLogic.validateIsolateRepayBasic and IsolateLogic.executeIsolateRepay), same mechanism (missing owner-onBehalf check), same impact (desynchronized accounting and underflow), and proposes the same fix (require tokenData.owner == onBehalf). Fixing as suggested would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The report explicitly flags the same issue: in VaultLogic.erc721DecreaseIsolateSupplyOnLiquidate the lockerAddr is not cleared, so a later redeposit inherits a stale lock and withdrawals/mode changes fail. The section titled “Stale locker state in VaultLogic.erc721DecreaseIsolateSupplyOnLiquidate can trap redeposited NFTs” matches the described code path, mechanism, impact, and proposes clearing/deleting the locker state—fixing the same root cause as [H-03]. Therefore, fixing the report’s issue also fixes the described vulnerability.

Yes. The report’s “Double-Counting of totalExtraAmount in IsolateLogic.executeIsolateLiquidate” describes the same root cause and code path: in executeIsolateLiquidate, line 464 subtracts vars.totalBorrowAmount from debtAssetData.totalBidAmout even though only the bid amounts were escrowed, which can underflow/revert after interest accrues during the auction. It proposes subtracting only the escrowed bids (effectively bidAmount = totalBorrowAmount - totalExtraAmount), which is the same fix as the description’s recommendation to decrease totalBidAmout by the bid amount. Same function, same lines, same mechanism, same fix.

Not detected. The described issue is an interface incompatibility: Ether.fi’s WithdrawRequestNFT.safeMint mints an ERC721 to the YieldAccount, which lacks onERC721Received (ERC721Receiver), causing requestWithdraw to revert and blocking unstake. The audit content discusses different failures around Ether.fi integration (wrong YieldAccount selection in protocolRequestWithdrawal/claimWithdraw, share vs asset mismatch, zero-amount issues, etc.) but does not mention ERC721Receiver/onERC721Received or safeMint compatibility. Fixes proposed in the report (using sd.yieldAccount, correcting denomination, etc.) would not address the missing ERC721Receiver; conversely, adding ERC721Receiver would not fix the report’s issues. Therefore, the specific vulnerability was not detected.

Yes. The audit content explicitly identifies the same issue: in IsolateLogic.executeIsolateLiquidate, there is no validation that params.msgSender equals loanData.lastBidder, and the function transfers the NFT to params.msgSender (lines ~472–478). It explains that any caller can liquidate after auction end and receive the NFT, and recommends restricting to the winning bidder or routing the NFT to lastBidder. This matches the described vulnerability’s mechanism, code path, and fix.

Yes. The audit content explicitly flags the same root cause and code paths: in _unstake (around line 312) and _repay (around line 384) the contract resolves the yield account via yieldAccounts[msg.sender], which breaks when botAdmin calls these functions, preventing forced unstake/repay. The report’s fixes (use sd.yieldAccount or the borrower’s account) address the same flaw, so fixing as suggested would also fix the vulnerability described.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports that LandManager.transferToUnoccupiedPlot fails to update toilerState[tokenId].plotId, causing plot occupancy inconsistencies. This is the same root cause, in the same function/code path, as the described issue (“single plot can be occupied by multiple renters”). Both scenarios arise from the stale plotId in toilerState, leading to double-occupancy/incorrect occupancy tracking. The proposed fix in both (setting toilerState[tokenId].plotId = plotId) is the same, so fixing the audit’s finding would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly includes “Off-by-one Plot Capacity Check in LandManager._farmPlots Allows Renters on Invalidated Plots to Farm Indefinitely,” which points to the same code path (LandManager._farmPlots around lines 258–260) and the same flaw (using < instead of <= when comparing _getNumPlots(landlord) to _toiler.plotId). It describes the exact boundary case where plotId 0 remains farmable after the landlord’s plots drop to 0 and recommends the same fix (change < to <=). Fixing that audit-identified issue would fix the vulnerability described.

Yes. The audit report’s section “Misplaced Parentheses in LandManager._farmPlots Bonus Calculation…” describes the same issue: incorrect parenthesization in the bonus application makes schnibblesTotal negative for negative finalBonus, which when cast to uint256 leads to an overflow on the subsequent tax multiplication and causes _farmPlots to revert. Because unstakeMunchable uses forceFarmPlots, this blocks unstaking of all NFTs. The proposed fix (move the /100 to only the bonus term) matches the vulnerability description’s fix. Same root cause, code path, impact, and remediation.

Yes. The audit explicitly describes the same root cause and code path: when PRICE_PER_PLOT is increased via configUpdated/_reconfigure, _getNumPlots decreases and in _farmPlots, if (_getNumPlots(landlord) < _toiler.plotId) the code sets timestamp = plotMetadata[landlord].lastUpdated, which can be earlier than _toiler.lastToilDate, causing (timestamp - _toiler.lastToilDate) to underflow and revert. This results in DoS/freezing of stake/unstake/farm—exactly the H-04 scenario. The proposed fix (tracking/snapshotting price-per-plot updates and clamping timestamp to avoid underflow) would also fix the vulnerability in the description. Same vulnerability type, same function and lines, same mechanism, and same effective remediation.

Yes. The audit explicitly reports that transferToUnoccupiedPlot fails to reset toilerState[tokenId].dirty to false (and to update lastToilDate), causing the token to be skipped in _farmPlots and preventing rewards after moving to a valid plot. It occurs in the same function/code path and the proposed fix (reset dirty and update lastToilDate) matches the vulnerability description’s remediation. Fixing the audit-reported issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report explicitly identifies the same issue: airdrop entitlement is assigned to initialOwners on mint/forge and not migrated on transfer, while burn (and thus NukeFund.nuke which calls burn) subtracts from initialOwners. This allows a buyer or later holder to burn/nuke and grief the original seller/minter’s airdrop balance. The report’s findings “Entitlement Attribution Mismatch Across Minting, Transfers, and Burns in Airdrop and TraitForgeNft” and “Incorrect Airdrop Entitlement Attribution via initialOwners…” reference the same functions and code path (TraitForgeNft._mintInternal/_mintNewEntity crediting initialOwners; TraitForgeNft.burn deducting from initialOwners; NukeFund.nuke invoking burn) and propose fixes (transfer entitlements on transfer or deduct from current owner / avoid deduction for non-initial owner) that would also remediate the described H‑02 griefing attack.

No. The vulnerability description is a math/logic error: incorrect percentage calculation when taxCut is changed (using amount/taxCut instead of a BPS-based percentage) in NukeFund.receive and EntityForging.forgeWithListed. The audit content discusses different issues: premature reset timer logic, off-by-one quota check, lack of refund for excess ETH, CEI violations and push-payment DoS in EntityForging, and synchronous payout DoS in NukeFund (including zero-value call reverts). None of the findings call out the incorrect taxCut percentage computation or propose the BPS-based fix. Fixes suggested in the report (pull payments, CEI, refunds) would not address the percentage miscalculation, and vice versa. Therefore, the specific vulnerability was not detected.

Yes. The audit content includes a dedicated section “Missing chainId Validation in PhiFactory.signatureClaim Enables Cross-Chain Signature Replay” that matches the described issue. It explains that signatureClaim decodes caller-provided encodeData_ and ignores the chainId field, enabling direct calls to replay a signature from another chain. It references the same function/lines, attack path (bypassing Claimable), and proposes the same fix (validate chainId or reconstruct with block.chainid). Fixing as proposed would resolve the reported vulnerability.

Yes. The audit’s first finding precisely matches the described issue: in PhiFactory.createArt, the signature only covers (expiresIn, uri, credData) and omits CreateConfig and msg.sender, enabling anyone to frontrun/replay a valid signature with arbitrary CreateConfig (artist/receiver/mintFee) and hijack royalties/ownership. Both describe the same code path (_validateArtCreationSignature -> createArt), same root cause (missing parameter binding and replay protection), same attack (reuse/front-run signature to set attacker as artist/receiver), and similar remediations (bind CreateConfig and caller to the signature, add nonce/used-signature tracking). Fixing what the report proposes would also fix the vulnerability described.

Yes. The audit explicitly flags that _updateCuratorShareBalance sets zero balances with EnumerableMap.set instead of removing the key, causing unbounded growth of shareBalance[credId_] and DoS of reward distribution that iterates over shareBalance via getCuratorAddresses/_getCuratorData. It proposes the same fix (remove the key when balance reaches zero). This is the same root cause, code path, impact, and remediation as the described [H-03] vulnerability.

Yes. The audit’s first finding (“Mint-window reopening in PhiFactory.updateArtSettings enables mints after an art’s deadline”) is the same issue. Both describe that updateArtSettings allows changing endTime without checking the previously stored art.endTime, so after a window has ended the creator can set a new future endTime, effectively reopening minting. The user report frames it as a ‘forced’ extension when updating other fields (URI/soulBounded/royalties) due to the EndTimeInPast check, which opens a backrun window for merkleClaim; the audit explicitly notes unrelated metadata updates shouldn’t require reopening and recommends treating ended windows as terminal or adding a dedicated, pre-deadline extension path. Same function and code path, same root cause (missing guard against modifying a finished schedule), same consequence (post-deadline mints), and the same remediation would fix both.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports reentrancy during createCred via the refund in _handleTrade, before credIdCounter is incremented, allowing re-entry into createCred and overwriting creds[credIdCounter] (including bondingCurve). This is the same code path and root cause as H-06. The suggested fixes (nonReentrant on the shared trade path and/or createCred, and incrementing credIdCounter before the external call) would also prevent the H-06 draining scenario that relies on overwriting the bonding curve mid-creation. While the audit focuses on ID collision/state overwrite (and notes pricing side effects), it covers the same vulnerability mechanism and location enabling the described drain.

Yes. The report explicitly identifies the same root flaw in the same code path (PhiFactory.updateArtSettings): unrestricted, post-creation edits to critical parameters. It covers (1) toggling soulBounded after mint (locking or unlocking transfers) and (2) unbounded royaltyBPS allowing excessively high royalties (including via CreatorRoyaltiesControl), and shows how this immediately impacts transfers in PhiNFT1155.safeTransferFrom. The proposed fixes (make soulBounded immutable after mint and cap royaltyBPS) align with the contest finding. While the contest finding also mentions URI changes, the core vulnerability—unrestricted updates to critical settings via updateArtSettings—was detected by the report.

Yes. The report’s section “Premature Withdrawal Execution Prior to Batch Expiry in WildcatMarketWithdrawals._executeWithdrawal Corrupts Batch Entitlement Accounting on Closed Markets” describes the same issue as H-01: when the market is closed, _executeWithdrawal allows withdrawals before batch expiry, then additional requests can still be added to the batch, altering batch.scaledTotalAmount and batch.normalizedAmountPaid after an early user has already withdrawn. This lets early users withdraw more than their eventual pro‑rata share and causes later users’ withdrawals to revert due to insufficient state.normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals (breaking the invariant that total withdrawals ≤ batch.normalizedAmountPaid). Same function/code path (_executeWithdrawal’s expiry check), same mechanism (premature execution on closed markets with subsequent changes to batch composition/rounding), same impact (last user fails), and the same fix (require expiry < block.timestamp or force immediate expiry on close).

Yes. The audit content explicitly identifies the pooled-escrow/stepsClaimed inheritance flaw in SecondSwap_StepVesting._createVesting when listings are transferred to SecondSwap_VestingManager (address(this)), where the first listing sets manager.stepsClaimed and subsequent listings ignore their own stepsClaimed. Buyers with no prior allocation then inherit manager.stepsClaimed on purchase, causing immediate-claim or no-claim outcomes depending on which listing was first. This matches the described issue that listing order affects how much buyers can claim at a given step. The audit covers the same code path (transferVesting to manager and _createVesting’s new-beneficiary branch) and mechanism, and proposes fixes that would also address the reported vulnerability.

Yes. The audit’s “Incorrect Schedule Merging and Release Rate Calculation in _createVesting” describes the same root flaw and code path: transferVesting -> _createVesting mismanages stepsClaimed. It highlights that _createVesting ignores the incoming _stepsClaimed when merging into an existing vesting (else-branch), explicitly noting the VestingManager pooling case where a single stepsClaimed (often 0) is kept and reused. This stale/global stepsClaimed then gets propagated to buyers via transferVesting, enabling premature claims—exactly the H‑02 scenario where new users adopt an incorrect stepsClaimed and can unlock tokens early. Both issues involve the same functions (transferVesting/_createVesting) and exploit the same mechanism (incorrect stepsClaimed propagation/merging), and addressing stepsClaimed handling in _createVesting (or tracking per-allocation/transfer) would fix both.

Yes. The audit’s section “Incorrect releaseRate recalculation in SecondSwap_StepVesting.transferVesting allows grantors to overclaim tokens via claim()” is the same vulnerability as [H-03]. It cites the same function and line (transferVesting, L230), explains the same root cause (releaseRate recomputed as totalAmount/numOfSteps ignoring amountClaimed and stepsClaimed), describes the same exploit path (overclaim via claim() before final step), and proposes the same fix ((totalAmount - amountClaimed)/(numOfSteps - stepsClaimed)). Fixing the issue as suggested in the report would fix the vulnerability described.

Yes. The report explicitly identifies that LiquidRon.totalAssets() does not subtract operatorFeeAmount, causing inflated totalAssets/share price and unfair outcomes across deposits/withdrawals. Two sections (“Unaccounted operatorFeeAmount…” and “LiquidRon.totalAssets fails to deduct operatorFeeAmount…”) describe the same root cause, code path (LiquidRon.totalAssets with operatorFeeAmount set in harvest/harvestAndDelegateRewards and realized in fetchOperatorFee), impacts (loss/dilution for new depositors and share-price drop on fee withdrawal), and propose the same fix (subtract operatorFeeAmount in totalAssets). Fixing as suggested in the report would also fix the vulnerability in the description.

Yes. The report has a dedicated finding “Unchecked domainSeparator in Forwarder._verifySig Enables Cross-Chain and Cross-Contract Signature Replay,” which matches the same mechanism: Forwarder._verifySig takes a caller-supplied domainSeparator, enabling cross-chain/cross-contract replay if nonces match. It cites the same functions (execute/_verifySig/_getEncoded) and recommends computing/validating the domain separator on-chain. The report also has a separate finding “Missing Expiration Deadline…” covering the lack of deadline checks that makes signatures indefinitely valid. Fixes proposed (enforce on-chain EIP-712 domain separator and add deadline) would resolve the described vulnerability. Therefore, the audit content detected the same issue.

Yes. The audit report explicitly covers the same issue: deposits/entitlement issuance are uncapped so totalTitnClaimable (+ totalTitnClaimed) can exceed the fixed TITN_ARB reserve, causing insolvency and an underflow in withdrawRemainingTitn when remainingTitnAfter1Year < initialTotalClaimable. It identifies the same code path (onTokenTransfer lines ~81–83 updating claimable/total without a cap; withdrawRemainingTitn computing remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable) and the same outcomes (late claimers fail; post-1-year withdrawals revert). The proposed fixes (cap by TITN_ARB or TGT_TO_EXCHANGE in onTokenTransfer/quoteTitn) match the vulnerability description’s suggested remedies. Thus, fixing the report’s issue would also fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report explicitly identifies the same sqrt bug: in Float128.sqrt’s 512-bit branch, rMan normalization (dividing by 10 and ++rExp when rMan > MAX_L_DIGIT_NUMBER) is performed before halving the exponent, causing the +1 adjustment to be lost and yielding a 10x (off-by-one exponent) error. It cites the same lines (around 735–742), the same root cause (order of operations), the same manifestation (incorrect exponent), and proposes the same fix (halve rExp before the rMan > MAX_L_DIGIT_NUMBER adjustment). This matches the vulnerability description exactly in code path, mechanism, and remediation.

Yes. The audit explicitly identifies the use of stop() in Float128.sqrt when a == 0 (same lines and function), explains that it halts the entire call frame with empty return data, and recommends returning 0 instead. This matches the described vulnerability’s mechanism, code path, impact, and fix.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports the same issue: Ln.ln accepts zero and negative inputs without checking the sign bit or zero (Missing Non-Positive Input Check in Ln.ln / Missing Domain Validation in Ln.ln and Ln.ln_helper). It points to Ln.sol lines 63–77, explains that MANTISSA_SIGN_MASK is ignored and zero is not validated, shows PoCs where ln(|x|) or a finite value is returned for invalid inputs, and recommends reverting on non-positive inputs. This is the same code path, root cause, impact, and remediation as the vulnerability description, so fixing the report’s issue would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content includes a dedicated finding “Incorrect Equality Comparison in Float128.eq Fails for Equivalent M-Size and L-Size packedFloat Representations” that identifies the exact issue: eq compares raw unwrapped uint256 values (lines 1070–1072) and thus fails when equal numbers are encoded with different mantissa sizes (M vs L) due to the L_MANTISSA_FLAG and differing exponent/mantissa fields. It proposes normalizing operands similarly to other comparison functions—same root cause, same code path, and same fix as the described [H-04] issue. Fixing the audit’s finding would fix the reported vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content’s section “Inconsistent Normalization and Precision Selection in Float128.toPackedFloat Produces Noncanonical Encodings and Precision Loss” describes the same flaw: in toPackedFloat, the M/L decision is driven only by exponent, so mantissas with 39–71 digits are downscaled to 38 digits (M) and lose up to 34 digits of precision. It cites the same code region (around line 1102), explains that this truncation occurs when exponent + (digitsMantissa − 38) ≤ MAXIMUM_EXPONENT, and explicitly proposes the same fix (set isResultL when digitsMantissa > MAX_DIGITS_M). Although the audit additionally discusses noncanonical encodings and comparisons, the underlying issue, code path, and remediation match the reported [H-05] precision loss vulnerability.

Yes. The report explicitly identifies the same issue: anyone can call AgentNftV2.addValidator (no access control), pre-registering a validator for nextVirtualId before mint, and because mint() unconditionally calls _addValidator, the founder (or attacker-chosen address) is inserted twice. The findings “Pre-Registration State Contamination and Duplicate Validator Initialization in AgentNftV2.mint” and “Missing Uniqueness Check in ValidatorRegistry._addValidator” match the described attack path and impact, noting duplicate validator entries and double-counting into validatorPoolRewards in AgentRewardV2._distributeValidatorRewards, which can later be withdrawn via withdrawValidatorPoolRewards causing accounting shortfalls. Although the report’s suggested fixes (dedupe and require minted) differ from the description’s proposed access control, both would prevent the same exploit; fixing the report’s issue would fix the described vulnerability. Same mechanism, code path, and impact.

Yes. The report explicitly flags the same root cause: ServiceNft.updateImpact is publicly callable with no access control, allowing anyone to arbitrarily recompute and overwrite impacts for a given virtualId/proposalId. Multiple sections describe how this manipulates getImpact used by AgentRewardV2._distributeContributorRewards and Minter.mint, leading to inflated/zeroed rewards—exactly the cascading effects described. The code path (ServiceNft.updateImpact) and exploitation mechanism (public visibility enabling arbitrary impact changes) match, and the proposed fix (make updateImpact internal/private) is the same. Fixing as suggested in the report would fix the vulnerability in the description.

Yes. The report repeatedly flags the same core issue in the same code path (ContributionNft.mint) — that untrusted, user‑supplied fields (notably datasetId and parentId, plus weak binding to the intended DAO/proposal) are accepted without validation and are then trusted downstream by ServiceNft.updateImpact, ServiceNft.mint and Minter.mint, leading to impact corruption and unauthorized token minting. Specifically, “Missing datasetId Validation in ContributionNft.mint…”, “Missing parentId Validation…”, and “Lack of Proposal Binding and Cross‑DAO Proposal ID Isolation…” describe the same mechanism and attack surface the vulnerability points to (proposers minting with bogus values causing cascading loss of funds). The report also traces identical impacts through ServiceNft.updateImpact and Minter.mint. While the contest write‑up suggests an admin‑only gate as the fix, the report’s proposed remediations (strict validation/binding of proposalId, datasetId, parentId, and virtualId/core consistency) would also eliminate the same exploit path. Thus, same vulnerability and code path; different but sufficient remediation approach.

Yes. The audit report explicitly flags the same root flaw in ValidatorRegistry: _initValidatorScore sets a new validator’s base score to totalProposals and validatorScore/getPastValidatorScore add that base to the DAO voting score. See Finding 12 (and also 8/11), which point to the exact functions (_initValidatorScore, validatorScore, getPastValidatorScore), explain that this lets validators appear at 100% participation (or even exceed totalProposals) without actual voting, and show how AgentRewardV2 uses this to overpay rewards. The recommended fixes (subtract current DAO score when initializing and/or cap the total at totalProposals, or initialize to 0) would also resolve the issue described in H-05. Same mechanism, same code path, same fix.

Yes. The audit’s first finding explicitly flags the lack of access control on GaugeFactoryCL.createGauge, shows that createGauge → createEternalFarming approves 1e10 of the reward token and that AlgebraEternalFarming pulls those tokens from GaugeFactoryCL, enabling repeated drains. It provides a PoC (“Bootstrap Fund Drainage”) and recommends restricting createGauge to an authorized caller—the same root cause, code path, impact, and fix as [H-02]. While the audit also discusses additional DoS/“confused-deputy” impacts, the token-drain mechanism and remediation exactly match the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly flags the exact bug in PanopticVaultAccountant.computeNAV at lines 134–136 where poolExposure1 is computed as longPremium.leftSlot() - shortPremium.leftSlot() instead of shortPremium.leftSlot() - longPremium.leftSlot(). It explains that shortPremium is an asset and longPremium a liability, shows the NAV impact on HypoVault fulfillDeposits/fulfillWithdrawals, cites the same code locations, and proposes the same fix (swap to shortPremium - longPremium). Fixing as the report suggests would also fix the vulnerability described.

Yes. The audit’s section “Unencumbered Vault Token Balances Added to Per-Pool Exposure…” describes the same flaw: direct wallet balances (including the underlying token when it appears in a pool) are added inside the per‑pool loop before applying Math.max(poolExposure0 + poolExposure1, 0), allowing negative, non‑recourse pool exposure to erase those balances. If the underlying token does not appear in any pool, it’s added after the loop (post‑clamp), creating inconsistent NAVs for identical economic positions depending on pool configuration. It cites the same code path (computeNAV around adding token0/token1 balances, the per‑pool clamp at line ~250, and the post‑loop underlying addition at lines ~254–258) and proposes a fix that separates/clamps pool exposures from wallet balances—fixing the inconsistency exactly as the vulnerability description requires. Thus, fixing the reported issue would also fix [H‑02].

Yes. The audit content explicitly identifies the same flaw: a chained signature whose outer header does not set the 0x40 checkpointer flag causes recover to enter recoverChained with _checkpointer = address(0) and an empty snapshot; the inner (final) link can then set 0x40 to load the checkpointer while _ignoreCheckpointer = true, so snapshotFor is never called and snapshot validation is skipped. This matches the described H-01 bypass exactly (same functions/lines in BaseSig.recover and recoverChained, same mechanism, same attack outcome). The suggested remediations (e.g., forbidding inner override of _checkpointer when _ignoreCheckpointer is true, or requiring 0x40 for chained signatures) would fix both.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports “Lack of Batch and Context Binding in SessionSig.hashCallWithReplayProtection Enables Batch Truncation, Extension, and Cross-Batch Signature Recombination,” pointing to SessionSig.recoverSignature and hashCallWithReplayProtection. It explains that each call is signed in isolation (hash includes only chainId/space/nonce/callIdx/hashCall) so an attacker can truncate or recombine batches—exactly the partial replay/frontrunning scenario described. It cites the same code path (SessionSig.recoverSignature lines 169–170 and hashCallWithReplayProtection), the same mechanism (missing binding to the full payload/batch), and proposes the same fix (bind the signature to the full payload context). Fixing what the report recommends would also fix the vulnerability described.

Yes. The audit content explicitly reports “Reentrancy in FeeAMM.burn via External Token Transfers Before State Updates Allows Draining Pool Reserves,” which matches the described vulnerability: a CEI violation in FeeAMM.burn where external token transfers occur before updating liquidityBalances, totalSupply, and reserves, enabling reentrancy via token hooks. Both reference the same function and code path, the same mechanism (reentrancy through token callbacks while state is stale), similar exploit narrative (nested burns extracting more than fair entitlement), acknowledge Solidity 0.7.x behavior, and propose the same fixes (reorder state updates before external calls and/or add nonReentrant). Fixing the issue as in the report would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit report explicitly flags that openChannel allows authorizedSigner == address(0) and that settle compares the recovered signer directly to authorizedSigner without checking for address(0), noting that recovery returns address(0) for invalid signatures. This matches the described zero-address signer validation bypass via address(0) recovery in the same functions (openChannel, settle, and also mentions close). The proposed remediations (reject authorizedSigner == address(0) and revert if recovered signer == address(0)) are the same fixes; addressing them in the report would fix the described vulnerability.

Yes. The audit content explicitly identifies that StablecoinDEX.cancel lacks an authorization check to ensure msg.sender is the order maker, allowing anyone to cancel any order. It points to the same function and code path, demonstrates that only OrderDoesNotExist is checked, and recommends the same fix (revert Unauthorized when msg.sender != order.maker). This matches the vulnerability description (H-02) in mechanism, location, impact, and remediation.

Yes. The audit’s second finding (“Missing Balance Validation and Unchecked Underflow in emergencyWithdraw and _processWithdrawal Allow Complete Protocol Drain”) describes the exact same issue as the vulnerability description: emergencyWithdraw calls _processWithdrawal without balance checks, and _processWithdrawal performs unchecked subtraction on user balances (and totalDeposits), enabling an underflow and allowing an attacker to withdraw more than their balance and drain the DEX. Same functions, same mechanism (unchecked underflow due to missing precondition checks), same attack path, and same remediation (add balance check, remove/guard unchecked).
